findings.text: The opening paragraph says what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves, in plain words. A newcomer can say what it is and why it matters after this one paragraph.
findings.source: Header lede: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: The first section after the navigation is an error message. The lede promises models, a verdict and costs, and this is where the newcomer would see them, so the page's main proof is missing and the page looks broken.
findings.source: Check it on a real job: "The records of job 20261029-073603-7kqv could not be read here, so no models, verdict or costs are shown: no reading record for job 20261029-073603-7kqv."

findings.text: Someone who arrives at Athena's home page finds that almost all of it describes another project, firstmate. The third lede paragraph explains this, but the title alone does not tell a newcomer that the page is an example of what Athena produces.
findings.source: Title and h1: "Athena explains how firstmate handles work"

findings.text: This link is aimed at the repository owner and sits in the header a newcomer reads first. Without context, "your decision" is confusing to a visitor.
findings.source: Header: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: Next steps are concrete: prerequisites, clone, `./setup.sh`, and a first command, with a note on what that command acts on. The header link also leads here, so a newcomer knows what to do next. The page does not say which operating systems are supported, or what accounts or API costs running it requires.
findings.source: Next steps: "git 2.40 or later; a C linker (cc)...; curl...; Claude Code, or npm to install it." and "athena ask \"add a changelog\"... press Enter to run it on that repository."

findings.text: Before the firstmate material says what firstmate is in any detail, the reader has to take in seven terms of jargon. The study content after that is dense: exit codes, places-held, pending-close records. It reads as reference material more than as a newcomer's introduction.
Several glossary entries say only that a term is undefined. The honesty fits the page's traceability claim, but a newcomer is left without a working meaning for those words.
findings.source: Glossary: "The firstmate source does not define a captain call." / "The firstmate source does not define a durable record."

findings.text: The page delivers on its traceability claim: almost every statement links to a claim, and every claim links to file lines at the pinned commit. A sceptical newcomer can check the work this way.
findings.source: Header lede: "Each statement below ends with the id of the claim that supports it; the claims, with links to their sources, are listed at the end."
